records.reason: Card claimed CoT 'forces the model to explain its logic'. Generated reasoning is not a faithful trace of the computation, and the claim is unsupported. Qualified, and Zero-Shot-CoT added as a related citation rather than a separate competing card.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2201.11903 verified 2026-09-22 — Wei, Wang, Schuurmans et al., v1 2022-01-28.

set.title: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting
set.content: Chain-of-Thought prompting supplies worked examples that show intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer, which elicits step-by-step output from the model on new problems. Wei et al. reported improvements on arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning benchmarks, with gains concentrated in larger models; the paper frames this as an emergent effect of scale rather than a universal improvement. The widely used zero-shot variant ('Let's think step by step') comes from a separate paper, Kojima et al., and its headline numbers were measured on 2022-era models. Important caveat: the emitted reasoning is not a verified trace of how the answer was computed. Models can produce plausible reasoning that rationalises an answer reached another way, so a chain of thought should not be treated as an explanation or an audit trail. Use it to improve multi-step task accuracy, not to justify a result to a user.
set.summary: Elicits intermediate reasoning steps, which can improve accuracy on selected multi-step tasks.
set.best_for: Multi-step arithmetic, symbolic and commonsense reasoning where intermediate steps help.
set.limitations: Gains are benchmark- and scale-dependent, not universal. Emitted reasoning may rationalise rather than reveal the actual computation, so it is not an explanation or audit trail.
set.venue: arXiv preprint (NeurIPS 2022 publication not confirmed from the arXiv record)
set.authors: Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans, et al.

related_citations.label: Zero-Shot-CoT — Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
related_citations.note: Kojima et al., NeurIPS 2022. Origin of 'Let's think step by step'. Reported figures are on text-davinci-002 / PaLM-540B.

records.reason: Card said it 'ensures reliability' and recommended it for 'high-stakes fact questions'. Majority voting over samples cannot establish truth — it selects the most frequent answer, including when that answer is consistently wrong.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2203.11171 verified 2026-09-22 — Wang, Wei, Schuurmans et al., ICLR 2023.

set.title: Self-Consistency (CoT-SC)
set.content: Self-Consistency samples several independent chains of thought at non-zero temperature and returns the most frequent final answer instead of the first one generated. Wang et al. reported accuracy gains over single-path chain-of-thought on arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks. The mechanism assumes that correct reasoning paths converge on the same answer more often than incorrect ones do, which holds for problems with a single well-defined answer and degrades for open-ended generation. Two practical consequences: cost scales roughly linearly with the number of samples, and agreement is a measure of consistency, not correctness — a model that is confidently wrong will agree with itself. Aggregating votes is therefore an accuracy technique on benchmarks with verifiable answers, not a factuality guarantee, and it should not be presented to users as verification.
set.summary: Samples several reasoning paths independently and returns the most frequent answer.
set.best_for: Problems with one well-defined answer where extra inference cost is acceptable.
set.limitations: Cost scales with sample count. Agreement measures consistency, not truth — a consistently wrong model still produces a confident majority. Not suited to open-ended generation.
set.authors: Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, et al.

records.reason: Card implied ToT is a prompt asking for several simultaneous thoughts. It is a search procedure requiring an external controller, state evaluation and backtracking — not something a single prompt performs.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2305.10601 verified 2026-09-22 — Yao, Yu, Zhao et al., NeurIPS 2023 camera-ready.

set.title: Tree of Thoughts (ToT)
set.content: Tree of Thoughts generalises chain-of-thought into an explicit search. Intermediate 'thoughts' become nodes in a tree; the controlling program expands candidate next steps, asks the model to evaluate how promising each partial state is, and then searches — typically breadth-first or depth-first — with the ability to abandon a branch and backtrack. This requires orchestration code outside the prompt: a single prompt cannot branch, score states and backtrack on its own. Yao et al. evaluated it on deliberately search-shaped tasks including Game of 24, creative writing and mini crosswords, where it substantially outperformed chain-of-thought. The cost is the main constraint: each node costs generation calls and each evaluation costs more, so a ToT run can consume one to two orders of magnitude more tokens than a single chain-of-thought answer. Reach for it when a task genuinely has multiple candidate paths worth comparing, not as a default upgrade.
set.summary: Searches over branching intermediate steps with evaluation and backtracking, driven by a controller loop.
set.best_for: Problems with several candidate solution paths worth exploring and comparing, where extra cost is justified.
set.limitations: Requires orchestration code (branching, state evaluation, backtracking) — not achievable from a single prompt. Inference cost is often 10-100x a single CoT answer. Evaluated on search-shaped tasks; gains do not transfer automatically to ordinary generation.
set.authors: Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao, et al.

records.reason: KEEP the mechanism; normalize metadata (venue, canonical id, authors were all null) and add the scope limitation.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2205.10625 verified 2026-09-22 — Zhou, Schärli, Hou et al., ICLR 2023.

set.title: Least-to-Most Prompting
set.content: Least-to-Most prompting splits a problem into an explicit decomposition stage and a sequential solving stage. The model is first asked to list the sub-problems needed to answer the question, then each sub-problem is solved in order with previous answers supplied as context. Because each step sees the concrete results of earlier steps, the technique targets problems where a later step depends on an earlier numeric or factual answer — the case where single-pass chain-of-thought tends to skip or conflate steps. Zhou et al. reported strong gains on compositional generalisation benchmarks such as SCAN, along with symbolic manipulation and math word problems, notably on problems harder than those shown in the prompt examples. It costs at least two model calls and adds latency, and the decomposition itself can be wrong — a bad split produces confidently wrong sub-answers, so it suits problems with a clear dependency structure rather than open-ended tasks.
set.summary: Decomposes a problem into ordered sub-problems, then solves them in sequence feeding each answer forward.
set.best_for: Multi-step problems where a later step depends on an earlier sub-answer.
set.limitations: Requires multiple calls and added latency. An incorrect decomposition propagates into every later step. Evidence is from compositional and math benchmarks, not open-ended generation.
set.authors: Denny Zhou, Nathanael Schärli, Le Hou, et al.

records.reason: KEEP mechanism; normalize canonical identity and add scope limitation. Title corrected to match the published paper.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2310.06117 verified 2026-09-22 — 'Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs', Zheng, Mishra, Chen et al., ICLR 2024.

set.title: Step-Back Prompting
set.content: Step-Back prompting inserts an abstraction step before the answer: the model is asked to state the general principle, concept or higher-level question behind the specific problem, and only then to solve the concrete instance using that principle. The intent is to stop the model anchoring on surface details of the question. Zheng et al. evaluated it on STEM questions, knowledge-intensive QA and multi-hop reasoning, reporting gains over direct prompting and over chain-of-thought on those benchmarks with PaLM-2L and comparable models. It costs an extra call or an extra output section, and it helps most where a retrievable general principle actually exists — physics and chemistry questions, policy lookups, domain rules. On tasks with no meaningful abstraction layer, the step-back stage adds tokens and latency without a corresponding benefit, and a wrong abstraction can steer the concrete answer off course.
set.summary: Asks for the governing principle behind a question first, then answers the specific instance using it.
set.best_for: STEM, knowledge-QA and multi-hop questions where a general principle genuinely governs the specific case.
set.limitations: Adds a call or output section. Only helps where a real abstraction exists; a wrong abstraction misdirects the final answer. Evidence is from specific reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
set.authors: Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Swaroop Mishra, Xinyun Chen, et al.

records.reason: Soften 'strong default' framing; scope evidence to the evaluated zero-shot reasoning benchmarks.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2305.04091 verified 2026-09-22 — Wang, Xu, Lan et al., ACL 2023.

set.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting
set.content: Plan-and-Solve is a zero-shot prompting pattern that replaces 'Let's think step by step' with an instruction to first devise a plan, then carry it out step by step. An extended variant adds explicit directions to extract relevant variables and compute intermediate results, which targets the calculation errors and skipped steps that zero-shot chain-of-thought tends to produce. Wang et al. evaluated it on arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning datasets, reporting improvements over zero-shot CoT and performance approaching few-shot CoT on several of them — without needing any worked examples in the prompt. That last property is the practical appeal: it suits situations where no good few-shot examples are available. The evidence comes from a defined set of reasoning benchmarks with verifiable answers, so treat it as a strong zero-shot option for reasoning tasks rather than a general-purpose default for all prompts.
set.summary: Zero-shot pattern that asks for a plan first, then executes it step by step.
set.best_for: Zero-shot multi-step reasoning where no good few-shot examples are available.
set.limitations: Evidence is from arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning benchmarks, not general generation. Planning quality bounds the result; the plan itself is unverified.
set.authors: Lei Wang, Wanyu Xu, Yihuai Lan, et al.

records.reason: Must state that the loop requires a tool-capable runtime. A plain text prompt cannot perform external actions; the previous card implied otherwise. ReAct remains the ACTIVE inference-time tool-use technique (Toolformer is archived as training-time history).
records.verified_source: arXiv:2210.03629 verified 2026-09-22 — Yao, Zhao, Yu et al.; v3 is the ICLR 2023 camera-ready.

set.title: ReAct (Reason + Act)
set.content: ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with actions in a loop: the model emits a thought, then an action (such as a search query or API call), the runtime executes that action and returns an observation, and the cycle repeats until the model emits an answer. Reasoning lets the model plan and revise what to do next; the observations keep it anchored to retrieved facts rather than its own priors. Yao et al. evaluated it on HotpotQA and FEVER with a Wikipedia API, and on ALFWorld and WebShop for interactive decision-making, reporting reduced hallucination versus chain-of-thought alone on the knowledge tasks. The critical implementation point: ReAct is a loop your application runs, not a property of the prompt. Something outside the model must parse each action, actually execute it, and feed the observation back. A prompt formatted in ReAct style with no tool runtime behind it will produce plausible fabricated observations, which is worse than not using it at all.
set.summary: Interleaves reasoning with tool calls and observations in a runtime-driven loop.
set.best_for: Tasks needing live external information or actions, where a tool-executing runtime exists.
set.limitations: Requires a runtime that parses actions, executes them and returns real observations. Without one, the model fabricates observations. Quality depends on the tools and their failure handling.
set.authors: Shunyu Yao, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, et al.

records.reason: KEEP mechanism; normalize metadata and state the external-signal requirement, which the previous card omitted.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2303.11366 verified 2026-09-22 — Shinn, Cassano, Berman et al.

set.title: Reflexion (Verbal Reinforcement)
set.content: Reflexion gives an agent a memory of its own failures. After an attempt is scored, the model writes a short natural-language reflection on what went wrong, that reflection is stored in an episodic buffer, and subsequent attempts receive it as context. No weights are updated — the 'learning' is entirely in text carried across trials. Shinn et al. evaluated it on decision-making, reasoning and code generation, reporting large gains on HumanEval in particular. The load-bearing dependency is the feedback signal: Reflexion works best where an attempt can be objectively scored, such as unit tests passing, a task environment returning success or failure, or a checkable numeric answer. Where the only critic is the same model judging its own work with no external ground truth, the gains are far less reliable — reflection then risks reinforcing a confident mistake. Budget for repeated attempts, since the method only pays off across several trials.
set.summary: Agent writes natural-language reflections on failed attempts into memory to improve later retries.
set.best_for: Retry-friendly agent loops with an objective success signal — tests, environment rewards, checkable answers.
set.limitations: Depends on a reliable external scoring signal; self-judged reflection can reinforce errors. Requires multiple attempts, so cost and latency scale with trials.
set.venue: arXiv preprint (NeurIPS 2023 publication not confirmed from the arXiv record)
set.authors: Noah Shinn, Federico Cassano, Edward Berman, et al.

records.reason: Remove the universal '2-5 examples' rule, which is unsupported. Example count, order, relevance and correctness are task- and model-dependent.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2005.14165 verified 2026-09-22 — 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners', Brown, Mann, Ryder et al.

set.title: Few-Shot Prompting (In-Context Learning)
set.content: Few-shot prompting places worked input-output examples in the prompt so the model infers the intended mapping rather than relying on instructions alone. Brown et al. established the effect at scale with GPT-3, showing performance generally improving as more in-context examples are supplied. It is the most direct lever for controlling output format, tone and edge-case handling, because an example demonstrates a convention that prose struggles to specify precisely. There is no universal correct number of examples. The useful count depends on the task, the model, how much the examples differ from each other and the available context budget, and later work has shown results are also sensitive to example order, label correctness and how representative the examples are of the real input distribution. Treat example selection as something to test rather than a fixed recipe, and check that your examples actually cover the edge cases you care about — incorrect or unrepresentative examples propagate directly into outputs.
set.summary: Supplies worked examples so the model infers the intended format and behaviour.
set.best_for: Enforcing a specific output format, tone or convention that prose instructions specify poorly.
set.limitations: No universal example count. Sensitive to example order, relevance, diversity and label correctness. Consumes context budget; unrepresentative examples propagate into outputs.
set.venue: arXiv preprint (NeurIPS 2020 publication not confirmed from the arXiv record)
set.authors: Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Mann, Nick Ryder, et al.

records.reason: Narrow evidence to the evaluated GPT-4 / CNN-DailyMail setting and record preprint status. Previous card generalised to 'reports and transcripts' without support.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2309.04269 verified 2026-09-22 — 'From Sparse to Dense: GPT-4 Summarization with Chain of Density Prompting', Adams, Fabbri, Ladhak et al. Preprint; no newer canonical version found.

set.title: Chain-of-Density (CoD) Summarization
set.content: Chain-of-Density produces a summary through successive rewrites at a fixed length. The model writes an initial sparse summary, then repeatedly identifies salient entities missing from it and rewrites to include them without increasing the length, which forces compression: filler gives way to named entities and specifics. Adams et al. evaluated this on CNN/DailyMail news articles using GPT-4, and reported that human annotators preferred the denser intermediate steps over the sparse first pass — though preference fell away at the highest densities, where summaries became harder to read. Two scope caveats matter. The study used one model on one news-summarization dataset, so transfer to long reports, meeting transcripts or technical documents is plausible but unevidenced. And the paper is a preprint with no peer-reviewed version located. The mechanism is still a sound and cheap way to raise information density when a length ceiling is fixed; just treat the optimum number of rounds as something to tune, not as a published constant.
set.summary: Iteratively rewrites a fixed-length summary to add missing entities, raising information density.
set.best_for: Fixed-length summaries where information density matters more than easy readability.
set.limitations: Evaluated with GPT-4 on CNN/DailyMail news only — transfer to reports or transcripts is unevidenced. Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Highest densities reduce readability.
set.authors: Griffin Adams, Alexander Fabbri, Faisal Ladhak, et al.

records.reason: Repoint to the canonical ACL Findings 2024 version. Reframe as independent self-checking, not external fact-checking; remove 'verified answer' framing.
records.verified_source: aclanthology 2024.findings-acl.212 verified 2026-09-22 — Dhuliawala, Komeili, Xu et al., DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.212.

set.title: Chain-of-Verification (CoVe)
set.content: Chain-of-Verification runs a four-step loop over a single model: draft an answer, plan verification questions that would test the draft's claims, answer those questions independently, then revise the draft in light of the answers. The load-bearing detail is the independence — verification questions are answered without the draft in context, so the model is less likely to simply restate its original claim. Dhuliawala et al. evaluated this on Wikidata list questions, closed-book MultiSpanQA and longform biography generation, reporting reduced hallucination relative to a direct answer. What it is not is fact-checking. No external source is consulted; the model is re-interrogating its own parameters. If the underlying belief is wrong, independent questioning can return the same wrong answer with added confidence. Use CoVe to catch internal inconsistency and unsupported detail, and use retrieval against real documents when the requirement is actual factual grounding.
set.summary: Drafts, plans verification questions, answers them independently, then revises the draft.
set.best_for: Catching internal inconsistency and unsupported specifics in list, entity and longform answers.
set.limitations: Consults no external source — it cannot establish truth, only self-consistency. A confidently wrong belief can survive verification. Costs several model calls.
set.authors: Shehzaad Dhuliawala, Mojtaba Komeili, Jing Xu, et al.

records.reason: MERGE TARGET. Absorbs the principle-constrained critique/revision pattern from Constitutional AI (which is retired as a standalone card). Adds the TACL survey limitation on intrinsic self-correction.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2303.17651 verified 2026-09-22 — Madaan, Tandon, Gupta et al. Merged pattern from arXiv:2212.08073. Limitation from aclanthology 2024.tacl-1.78 (Kamoi et al., TACL vol. 12).

set.title: Self-Refine (Iterative Self-Feedback)
set.content: Self-Refine loops a single model through generate, critique, revise: it drafts, then is prompted separately to give specific actionable feedback on that draft, then rewrites using that feedback. Separating the critique turn from the revision turn is what makes it work — a combined 'improve this' instruction tends to produce cosmetic edits. Madaan et al. reported gains across tasks including code optimization, dialogue response and sentiment rewriting, with no additional training. A useful variant, drawn from the critique-and-revise stage of Constitutional AI, is to constrain the critique against an explicit written list of principles rather than leaving it open-ended: the model checks the draft against each stated rule, then revises. This makes the pass auditable and repeatable, and it is the practical way to enforce style, policy or safety conventions at inference time. The important limitation is that prompted self-correction is unreliable without a dependable signal. A critical TACL survey found no convincing evidence that models reliably correct their own reasoning errors from self-generated feedback alone; self-correction works best where feedback is externally grounded — tests, validators, retrieved sources — or where the task is easy to verify but hard to produce.
set.summary: Generate, critique, revise with one model — optionally constraining the critique against explicit written principles.
set.best_for: Polishing drafts, code and writing, and enforcing explicit style or policy rules at inference time.
set.limitations: Prompted self-correction is unreliable without external grounding; a TACL survey found no convincing evidence of reliable intrinsic reasoning self-correction. Costs at least two extra calls. The full Constitutional AI method additionally uses supervised fine-tuning and RLAIF and is NOT prompting-only.
set.venue: arXiv preprint (NeurIPS 2023 publication not confirmed from the arXiv record)
set.authors: Aman Madaan, Niket Tandon, Prakhar Gupta, et al.

records.reason: Repoint to canonical EMNLP 2023 version. Add the self-preference/evaluator-bias warning the authors state. Remove the implicit recommendation to surface judge chain-of-thought.
records.verified_source: aclanthology 2023.emnlp-main.153 verified 2026-09-22 — Liu, Iter, Xu, Wang, Xu, Zhu. DOI 10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.153. Abstract explicitly flags evaluator bias toward LLM-generated text.

set.title: G-Eval (LLM-as-a-Judge)
set.content: G-Eval scores generated text with an LLM judge by combining an explicit evaluation rubric with a structured form-filling output, so the judge returns a defined score per named criterion rather than a loose opinion. Liu et al. evaluated it on text summarization and dialogue generation with GPT-4 and reported higher correlation with human judgements than prior automatic metrics. For building a judge, the transferable lessons are to define criteria explicitly, give each a calibrated scale with anchors, and require a short concrete justification tied to specific evidence in the text. The authors flag a serious limitation directly: LLM evaluators show bias toward LLM-generated text, meaning a judge can systematically favour machine output — including output from a model like itself. Treat judge scores as a comparative signal within a fixed setup, not an absolute quality measure, and calibrate against human ratings before trusting them. Keep the judge's internal deliberation out of user-facing output; publish the criterion scores and brief evidence instead.
set.summary: LLM judge combining an explicit rubric with structured per-criterion scoring.
set.best_for: Designing reference-free evaluation rubrics and calibrated LLM judges.
set.limitations: Authors report evaluator bias toward LLM-generated text, so scores can systematically favour machine output. Scores are comparative within a fixed setup, not absolute; calibrate against human ratings. Judge deliberation should not be exposed to end users.
set.authors: Yang Liu, Dan Iter, Yichong Xu, et al.

records.reason: KEEP as a core APO method. Add the requirement for representative scoring data and held-out evaluation, and the optimizer-overfitting risk. Title corrected to the published title with OPRO as an alias.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2309.03409 verified 2026-09-22 — 'Large Language Models as Optimizers', Yang, Wang, Lu et al., ICLR 2024. OpenReview Bb4VGOWELI is bot-walled; stable proceedings URL recorded as related.

set.title: OPRO — Large Language Models as Optimizers
set.content: OPRO uses an LLM as the optimizer in a search loop over prompts. Each round, the optimizer model receives the task description plus a trajectory of previously tried instructions and their measured scores, and proposes new candidate instructions; those are scored and fed back, so the trajectory itself becomes the optimization signal. Yang et al. demonstrated the idea on small toy problems (linear regression, travelling salesman) and applied it to prompt optimization, reporting gains over human-written prompts on GSM8K and Big-Bench Hard. Two requirements are non-negotiable in practice. You need a scoring function and a representative set of scored examples — without a metric there is nothing to optimize against. And you need a held-out evaluation set, because the loop optimizes directly against the scores it sees and will happily overfit to a small or unrepresentative training subset, producing an instruction that scores well in the loop and disappoints in production. Budget for many scored generations per round.
set.summary: Uses an LLM as an optimizer, proposing new instructions from a trajectory of scored prior attempts.
set.best_for: Automatically searching for higher-scoring instructions when a reliable metric and scored examples exist.
set.limitations: Requires a scoring function and representative scored data. Optimizes against observed scores, so it overfits small or unrepresentative sets — a held-out evaluation set is mandatory. High evaluation-call volume.
set.authors: Chengrun Yang, Xuezhi Wang, Yifeng Lu, et al.

set.title: Skeleton-of-Thought (SoT)
set.content: Skeleton-of-Thought targets end-to-end latency rather than answer quality. The model first emits a terse skeleton — a list of point headings for the answer — and each point is then expanded into full text. The saving comes from expanding those points concurrently, as parallel requests or a batched call, so wall-clock time is bounded by the slowest point rather than the sum of all of them. Ning et al. reported speed-ups across a range of models, with quality effects varying by question type: improvements on some categories and regressions on others, particularly where the answer needs continuous argument rather than enumerable parts. The critical implementation detail is that the gain is architectural, not prompt-magic. Asking one model to write an outline and then expand it sequentially in the same conversation produces no speed-up at all — it produces more tokens and therefore takes longer. Use it only where your runtime can genuinely issue the expansions in parallel and the answer decomposes into independent sections.
set.summary: Emits a point skeleton, then expands the points in parallel to cut wall-clock latency.
set.best_for: Enumerable, list-shaped answers where the runtime can genuinely expand sections concurrently.
set.limitations: The latency gain requires actual parallel or batched expansion — sequential outline-then-expand is slower, not faster. Quality varies by question type and can regress where an answer needs continuous argument.
set.authors: Xuefei Ning, Zinan Lin, Zixuan Zhou, et al.

set.title: Meta-Prompting (Task-Agnostic Scaffolding)
set.content: Meta-prompting in the Suzgun and Kalai sense is an orchestration pattern, not a single clever prompt. One model instance acts as a conductor: it decomposes the task, spawns fresh expert instances with narrowly scoped instructions, sends each a self-contained sub-request, then verifies and assembles their returned answers. Because each expert starts with a clean context, the pattern isolates sub-tasks from one another and gives the conductor a review point before results are combined. The authors evaluated it on Game of 24, Checkmate-in-One and Python Programming Puzzles, reporting gains over standard prompting. Two scope limits should be stated whenever this is cited. The evaluation used GPT-4 alone, so cross-model transfer is unevidenced. And the strongest configurations included a Python interpreter as one of the tools, so the reported gains are not attributable to the scaffolding in isolation. It is inherently multi-call and therefore materially more expensive and slower than a single request.
set.summary: A conductor model decomposes a task, delegates to fresh expert instances, then verifies and combines their output.
set.best_for: Decomposable tasks where isolating sub-problems in clean contexts and reviewing before assembly is worth extra cost.
set.limitations: Evaluated with GPT-4 only — cross-model transfer unevidenced. Best results included a Python interpreter, so gains are not attributable to scaffolding alone. Inherently multi-call: higher cost and latency.

records.reason: Overbroad card claimed personas improve output quality generally. Broad evaluations find generic personas do NOT reliably improve factual accuracy, and irrelevant persona detail actively harms. Rebuilt as a balanced mixed-evidence record distinguishing detailed task-specific expert identity from a generic role label.
records.verified_source: arXiv:2305.14688 (ExpertPrompting, Xu/Yang/Lin) + aclanthology 2024.findings-emnlp.888 (Zheng et al., 4 LLM families, 2410 questions, 162 roles) + aclanthology 2025.emnlp-main.1364 (Luz de Araujo et al., 9 LLMs x 27 tasks). All verified 2026-09-22.

set.title: Expert / Persona Prompting — Mixed Evidence
set.content: Assigning the model a role is one of the most common prompt moves and one of the least reliably beneficial. The evidence splits by specificity. ExpertPrompting showed that generating a detailed, task-specific expert identity — relevant background, and how such an expert would approach this particular request — and prepending it can improve response quality ratings. Broad evaluations of the generic version point the other way: Zheng et al. tested 162 role descriptions across four model families on 2,410 factual questions and found personas in system prompts did not reliably improve accuracy over no persona at all, with effects close to random. Luz de Araujo et al., across nine models and 27 tasks, found expert personas mostly neutral-to-positive but showed that irrelevant persona details can cause large accuracy drops. The practical reading: a detailed, genuinely relevant expert description is worth testing for tone, vocabulary and framing; a generic label such as 'You are a senior developer' should not be expected to improve factual correctness, and padding a persona with irrelevant biography can actively hurt.
set.summary: Detailed task-relevant expert descriptions may help; generic role labels do not reliably improve factual accuracy.
set.best_for: Steering tone, vocabulary and framing with a detailed, genuinely relevant expert description.
set.limitations: Generic personas did not reliably improve factual accuracy across 4 model families / 162 roles. Irrelevant persona detail can cause large accuracy drops. Benefits are mostly stylistic, not factual; automatic persona selection performs near-randomly.
set.authors: Benfeng Xu, An Yang, Junyang Lin, et al.

set.title: Structured Delimiters, including XML
set.content: Separating the parts of a prompt with consistent structural markers — XML-style tags, markdown headings or clearly named fenced sections — makes it unambiguous which text is an instruction, which is data to operate on, and which is an example. This matters most in long prompts that mix all three, where an instruction buried next to user-supplied content can be read as part of that content. It can reduce ambiguity between sections; it is not a security boundary and does not by itself prevent a model from following instructions embedded in user data. The strongest published guidance for XML tags specifically is vendor documentation from Anthropic for the Claude family, which reflects how those models were trained rather than a model-independent finding; other model families are generally documented as responding well to markdown structure. Treat the choice of marker as model-specific convention, keep it consistent within a prompt, and pair it with explicit instructions about how untrusted content should be treated.
set.summary: Consistent structural markers separate instructions, data and examples, reducing ambiguity in long prompts.
set.best_for: Long prompts mixing instructions, data and examples in one request.
set.limitations: Vendor guidance for XML tags is Claude-specific and reflects training conventions, not a model-independent result. Delimiters reduce ambiguity but are not a security boundary against injected instructions in user data.

set.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — Architecture
set.content: Lewis et al. introduced RAG as a trained architecture: a parametric generator (BART) combined with a non-parametric memory (a dense-vector Wikipedia index queried by DPR), fine-tuned end-to-end so the generator learns to use retrieved passages. They evaluated it on open-domain QA, abstractive QA, question generation and fact verification. This is worth stating precisely because the term has since drifted. What most systems call RAG today is a different, untrained pattern — retrieve passages with an embedding model, paste them into the context window of a frozen instruction-tuned model, and instruct it to answer from them. That pattern inherits the motivation of the original work (ground generation in retrievable evidence, update knowledge without retraining) but not its results, which were measured on a fine-tuned system. Practices layered on top of the modern pattern — requiring inline citations, instructing the model to abstain when the context does not contain the answer, constraining answers to quoted spans — are sensible implementation guidance derived from experience, and should be labelled as such rather than attributed to this paper.
set.summary: The original trained retrieve-and-generate architecture: parametric generator plus non-parametric dense index, fine-tuned end to end.
set.best_for: Background on why grounding generation in retrieved evidence works, and what the original result did and did not show.
set.limitations: Describes a FINE-TUNED architecture, not the frozen retrieve-then-prompt pattern now commonly called RAG. Citation, abstention and quoting practices are derived implementation guidance, not findings of this paper.
set.authors: Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandra Piktus, et al.
